lessons.title: Compute and hosting options: scale sets, desktops, containers, functions, and web apps
lessons.summary: Expands compute coverage with VM scale sets, availability sets, Azure Virtual Desktop, containers, Functions, and App Service.
learningObjectives: Compare VM scale sets, availability sets, Virtual Desktop, containers, Functions, and App Service
Choose an Azure compute option from hosting, scaling, and operations clues
Identify when Container Apps, Container Instances, or Functions fit an app workload
lessons.explanation: Azure compute choices depend on what is hosted and how much operation the team accepts. Virtual machines fit OS control. Virtual Machine Scale Sets fit groups of similar VMs that scale together. Availability sets help place related VMs across fault and update domains. Azure Virtual Desktop delivers hosted desktops or remote apps. For containers, Azure Container Instances is simple, Container Apps is managed and app-centric, and AKS is for Kubernetes orchestration. App Service hosts web apps and APIs with less server work. Azure Functions runs event-driven code.

terminology.definition: Groups of VM instances that can scale together.
VM placement across fault and update domains.
Hosted desktops and remote apps on Azure.

lessons.businessScenario: Relecloud runs a flash-sale storefront, a contractor desktop pool, a nightly containerized import, and an image-resize workflow triggered by uploads.
lessons.technicalExample: The storefront uses VM scale sets for a VM-based tier, contractors use Azure Virtual Desktop, the nightly import runs in Azure Container Instances, the API runs in Container Apps, and uploaded images trigger Azure Functions.

misconception.myth: Any container workload should immediately be placed on AKS.
misconception.reality: ACI, Container Apps, App Service, and AKS can all run containers; AKS is best when Kubernetes orchestration is truly needed.

lessons.examTakeaway: Choose compute by the clue: identical VM scaling, VM placement resilience, desktop virtualization, simple container, managed container app, Kubernetes, web app, or event-driven function.
lessons.recap: Expands compute coverage with VM scale sets, availability sets, Azure Virtual Desktop, containers, Functions, and App Service.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Compute choices are like delivery options: a rented truck for full control, a fleet for bursts, a courier for one container job, and a vending machine for event-triggered tasks.
lessons.anotherExample: A university uses App Service for admissions, Azure Virtual Desktop for temporary reviewers, ACI for a nightly transcript container, and Functions for file-arrival notifications.

lessons.title: Azure networking in depth: peering, DNS, hybrid connections, and endpoints
lessons.summary: Deepens networking with VNet peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, public endpoints, and private endpoints.
learningObjectives: Identify when to use VNet peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, or ExpressRoute
Distinguish public endpoints from private endpoints for Azure resources
Choose hybrid or private connectivity for branch and provider-network needs
lessons.explanation: Networking questions usually ask whether to connect, resolve, or reach. VNet peering connects Azure virtual networks. Azure DNS hosts DNS zones and records so apps can be reached by name. VPN Gateway supports encrypted VPN connectivity such as site-to-site and point-to-site. ExpressRoute provides private connectivity through a provider. A public endpoint is reachable through public addressing; a private endpoint gives a supported service a private IP in a VNet. Private endpoints reduce public exposure but do not replace identity, authorization, or monitoring.

terminology.definition: Provides VPN connectivity to Azure VNets.
Private IP access to a supported Azure service.

lessons.businessScenario: Fabrikam has separate hub, app, and data VNets. Branch offices need Azure access, users need friendly names, and a storage account should be reachable through private addressing only.
lessons.technicalExample: Engineers peer the hub and app VNets, publish app records in Azure DNS, use VPN Gateway for a branch pilot, evaluate ExpressRoute for provider-based private connectivity, and create a private endpoint for storage.

misconception.myth: A private endpoint is the same thing as an identity or authorization rule.
misconception.reality: A private endpoint changes network reachability by using a private IP; identity permissions, DNS, and monitoring still need separate configuration.

lessons.examTakeaway: Peering connects VNets, Azure DNS resolves names, VPN Gateway supports VPN tunnels, ExpressRoute provides private provider connectivity, and private endpoints reduce public network exposure for supported services.
lessons.recap: Deepens networking with VNet peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, public endpoints, and private endpoints.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Networking is a campus: peering opens roads between buildings, DNS provides signs, VPN is a secured tunnel, ExpressRoute is a private bus line, and a private endpoint is a staff-only entrance.
lessons.anotherExample: A hospital peers clinical and reporting VNets, uses Azure DNS for application names, and exposes a storage account to the app through a private endpoint.

lessons.title: Storage redundancy and access tiers through scenarios
lessons.summary: Adds storage scenario practice for redundancy and blob access tiers.
learningObjectives: Distinguish storage redundancy choices from blob access tiers
Choose hot, cool, cold, or archive tiers from blob access patterns
Identify resilience clues that point to zonal or geo-redundant storage
lessons.explanation: Storage settings answer different questions. Redundancy is about how Azure stores copies for resilience: locally redundant, zone-redundant, and geo-redundant choices reflect different replication patterns. Access tiers are about expected blob usage: hot for frequent access, cool or cold for less frequent access, and archive for rarely accessed data that can tolerate retrieval steps. If the scenario mentions zones, regions, copies, or disaster recovery, think redundancy. If it mentions frequently read or rarely read data, think access tier.

terminology.definition: The replication approach used to keep Azure Storage data durable and available.
Copies kept within a single datacenter location.
Copies stored across availability zones in one region.
Replication to a secondary region for broader recovery planning.
A setting that reflects expected read frequency and retrieval tolerance.

lessons.businessScenario: Northwind Traders stores active catalog images, quarterly audit exports, and daily order files. Each data set has a different access pattern and resilience requirement.
lessons.technicalExample: Architects put catalog images in the hot tier, move old audit exports to an archive-friendly lifecycle, and choose zone-redundant or geo-redundant storage based on the order-file recovery requirement.

misconception.myth: Choosing the archive tier also gives stronger regional resilience.
misconception.reality: Access tiers describe how often blob data is expected to be read; redundancy options describe how data is replicated.

lessons.examTakeaway: Zones, regions, copies, and disaster-recovery wording point to redundancy; frequently read, rarely read, or retained wording points to access tiers.
lessons.recap: Adds storage scenario practice for redundancy and blob access tiers.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Storage is like a museum: redundancy is how many buildings keep copies, while access tier is whether an item is on display, in the back room, or in deep archive.
lessons.anotherExample: A clinic stores today’s forms in hot storage, old scans in a cooler tier, and selects redundancy according to whether zone or regional recovery is required.
